parsing_res_list.block_content: parameterize the binary Tx map  $ C_{t} $ through the following relation:
$$ C_{t}(p,q)\triangleq\begin{cases}1,&\exists i\in\{1,\cdots,R\}s.t.(p,q)=(u_{t}^{i},v_{t}^{i}),\\0,&otherwise,\end{cases} $$

where  $ (u_t^i, v_t^i) = \text{round}(a_t^i, b_t^i) $. Thus  $ \Omega_t $ becomes the actual optimization variables that influence the RM generation through  $ C_t $, which serves as the input to the reverse diffusion process at step  $ t $. This parameterization dramatically reduces the variable dimension from  $ w \times h $ binary elements to  $ 2R $ continuous ones, significantly improving computational efficiency.
To further stabilize the reverse-time refinement, we introduce a best-anchor mechanism and optimize an augmented objective with a proximal regularization term:

$$ \begin{array}{r}{\mathcal{L}_{t}(\Omega_{t})=\left\|\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{0}^{t}(\Omega_{t})\odot\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}-\boldsymbol{O}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{\kappa_{t}}{2}\left\|\Omega_{t}-\Omega_{t}^{\star}\right\|_{F}^{2},}\end{array} $$
where  $ \Omega_{t}^{*} $ denotes the best Tx coordinates found up to time t,
$$ \Omega_{t}^{\star}\triangleq\underset{\Omega_{s},s\geq t}{\arg\min}\left\|\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{0}^{s}(\Omega_{s})\odot\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}-\boldsymbol{O}\right\|_{F}^{2}, $$
and  $ \kappa_{t} $ is a linearly scheduler defined as
$$ \kappa_{t}=\kappa\frac{T-t}{T},\kappa>0. $$
To minimize  $ \mathcal{L}_t(\Omega_t) $, we apply momentum-based gradient descent (GD) method to update the coordinates. For each horizontal coordinate  $ a_t^i $, the update is given by:

The quadratic term acts as a proximal pull, shrinking the search region toward the anchor and suppressing oscillations when the loss landscape becomes sharp at low noise levels. The linear schedule ensures that this pull is negligible during early exploratory stages and gradually strengthens as the noise level decreases. As shown later in Section V, the proposed best-anchor mechanism substantially enhances the recovery accuracy of RM estimation.
$$ v_{t-1}=\beta v_{t}+(1-\beta)\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{t}}{\partial a_{t}^{i}},\quad a_{t-1}^{i}=a_{t}^{i}-\eta v_{t-1}, $$
where  $ \eta > 0 $ is the learning rate and  $ \beta > 0 $ is the momentum coefficient. The same update rule is applied to the vertical coordinates  $ b_{t}^{i} $.
By the chain rule,  $ \frac{\partial L_{t}}{\partial a_{t}^{i}} $ is computed as

$$ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{t}}{\partial a_{t}^{i}}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{t}}{\partial\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{t}}\cdot\frac{\partial\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{t}}{\partial\mathbf{C}_{t}}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{C}_{t}}{\partial a_{t}^{i}}+\kappa_{t}\left(a_{t}^{i}-a_{t}^{i,\star}\right), $$

where  $ a_t^* $ is the horizontal coordinate of  $ \Omega_t^* $. The  $ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{x}_0} $ and  $ \frac{\partial \hat{x}_0^t}{\partial \mathcal{C}_t} $ can be easily obtained by back-propagation. As for  $ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a_t^*} $, note that the binary Tx map  $ \mathcal{C}_t $ is obtained by applying a non-differentiable operation, cf. Eqn. (6). This makes the gradient  $ \partial \mathcal{C}_t / \partial a_t^i $ undefined. To circumvent this difficulty, we introduce a smooth approximation  $ \hat{C}_t \in \mathbb{R}_+^{w \times h} $, formed by summing  $ R $ isotropic Gaussian heatmaps centered at each Tx location:
$$ \hat{C}_{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{R}\boldsymbol{P}_{t}^{i},\quad\boldsymbol{P}_{t}^{i}(j,k)=\exp\left(-\frac{(j-a_{t}^{i})^{2}+(k-b_{t}^{i})^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right), $$
where  $ \sigma $ is the standard deviation, which controls approximation accuracy. Particularly as  $ \sigma $ approaches 0, the soft map  $ \hat{C}_t $ converges to the binary Tx map  $ C_t $.
With this approximation, we adopt the straight-through estimator (STE) [19], [20] and approximate the backward gradient by differentiating through the soft map:

$$ \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{C}_{t}}{\partial a_{t}^{i}}\approx\frac{\partial\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}_{t}}{\partial a_{t}^{i}}=\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{P}_{t}^{i}}{\partial a_{t}^{i}}=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}(\boldsymbol{J}-a_{t}^{i})\odot\boldsymbol{P}_{t}^{i}, $$
where  $ J \in \mathbb{R}^{w \times h} $ is a row index matrix satisfying  $ J(j, k) = j $.

Thus far, we have completed the description of the two core components—RM generation and Tx update. Since the RM estimation problem is highly non-convex, the overall procedure is notably sensitive to the initialization of the Tx coordinates. In the following subsection, we introduce an efficient strategy to obtain a reliable initialization for  $ \Omega_{T} $.
### D. Initialization for Tx Coordinates  $ \Omega_{T} $

We propose a propagation-guided k-means (PG-KMeans) method to initialize the coordinates at $t = T$. The one-iteration visualization of the method is shown in Fig. 4. Let $\mathcal{S} = \{(m_k, n_k)\}$ be the set of sampled grid indices with $\mathcal{M}(m_k, n_k) = 1$, and recall that $\mathcal{O}(m_k, n_k)$ denote the measured RSS at those indices. Using a site-calibrated first-order path-loss model $o = p(d; \vartheta)$ with known parameters $\vartheta$, which is easy to get by preliminary investigation, we can map each RSS value to a range via the analytic inverse $d = \psi(o) = p^{-1}(o; \vartheta)$:
$$ d_{k}=\psi\big(\boldsymbol{O}(s_{k})\big),\qquad\mathbf{s}_{k}=\big(m_{k},n_{k}\big), $$

so that each sample $k$ specifies a circle of feasible Tx locations centered at $\mathbf{s}_k$ with radius $d_k$. Stacking the $R$ Tx positions into $\Omega = \{\omega_i \in \mathbb{R}^2\}_{i=1}^R$, we seek $\Omega$ that best fits all circles in a least-squares sense. A convenient surrogate is the range-consistency distortion
$$ \mathcal{F}(\Omega)\;=\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}}\operatorname*{m i n}_{1\leq i\leq R}\Big(\left\Vert\mathbf{s}_{k}-\boldsymbol{\omega}_{i}\right\Vert_{2}-d_{k}\Big)^{2}, $$
which measures how well each sample can be explained by its nearest Tx. Minimizing (13) is nonconvex but admits a fast alternating strategy that mirrors K-means while respecting propagation geometry.
Starting from random seeds  $ \{\omega_i^{(0)}\}_{i=1}^R $, we iterate three simple operations:

1) Assignment: For each sample $k$, compute $e_{k,i} = \left|\left\|\mathbf{s}_{k} - \boldsymbol{\omega}_{i}^{(\ell)}\right\|_{2} - d_{k}\right|$ and assign $k$ to cluster $\mathcal{E}_{i}^{(\ell)}$ that attains the minimum $e_{k,i}$.
2) Back-projection: For each  $ (k,i) $ with  $ k \in \mathcal{E}_i^{(\ell)} $, form a candidate Tx point by projecting  $ s_k $ onto its range circle along the ray toward the current center:

$$ \tilde{\boldsymbol{\omega}}_{k,i}=\mathbf{s}_{k}+d_{k}\cdot\frac{\boldsymbol{\omega}_{i}^{(\ell)}-\mathbf{s}_{k}}{\max\left\{\left\|\boldsymbol{\omega}_{i}^{(\ell)}-\mathbf{s}_{k}\right\|_{2},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right\}}, $$
with a small  $ \epsilon > 0 $ to avoid division by zero.
